That night Rue sits with you at the fire in the room Sorrel has found you, with her book open on her knees and a new stub of lead.

That night Rue comes to find you, with her book.

oneOf.text: You. Stood in the gate with me. Did not move.
You. Fought the white in the gate, so that I was not put out.

lines.text: Maren. Asked what I gave. Listened to me as if I might be lying, and then as if I was not.

lines.narrate: Maren laughs, surprised, and then stops, and looks at Rue for a long moment, the way she looks at people when she is listening for something and hears nothing at all.

lines.text: Nessa. Wanted the gate open before anyone. Talks to the dog.
He talks back.
I have written that too. Biscuit. Dog. Grey at the mouth. Kind.
Orin. Would not let them put me out.

lines.narrate: Orin goes quiet. He sits with his hands on his knees and looks at the fire, and does not say anything for so long that Rue looks up from her book to see whether she has written it wrong.

lines.text: Is it wrong? I can cross it out. I do not like to, but I can.
No. Leave it. Put the day beside it.

lines.narrate: She writes the day beside it. Orin watches her do it.
Then she closes the book, and holds it shut on her knees with both hands.

choices.label: Ask her what she wrote on her own page tonight
Build the fire up, and let her be

lines.narrate: Then the last line on her own page, in fresh lead, which she reads twice.

lines.text: I was let in.
We read our books before anything hard, so we know who we were before it. If I read it first, then whatever happens, I was somebody when it started. Tomorrow is hard. Everything here is.

oneOf.narrate: Somewhere below, under the gatehouse, Hesk is reading over to himself the speech he gave at his appeal today. You can hear his voice through the floor, steady, not the words.
Up on the wall the watch-fire at the head of the north road is lit again, and somebody is sitting by it.

choices.label: Sleep

lines.narrate: You sleep. When you wake in the grey before dawn Rue is already awake, sitting up with her book, reading yesterday again.

choices.label: Ask her to show you how she makes her letters

lines.narrate: She shows you. Square, joined at the shoulder, every letter standing up against the next one as if it might fall without it. You make your name in it, badly, in the margin of her page.

lines.text: That is terrible. I will keep it.

records-camp.location: The archive under the toll-house, Ashford Crossing

lines.narrate: Ilse does not sleep that night either, and neither does Rue. They sit at opposite ends of the long table in the cellar with a lamp each, copying: Ilse the founders' account in her round archive hand, and Rue the Wold's winters in her square one.
Rue goes back up to Highpass on the morning coach. Brannagh wants her home by the end of the week, and Rue has written it on the back of her hand so as not to forget.
Sorrel's rider takes Rue back up to Highpass in the morning. Sorrel wants her at the fire, and Rue has written it on the back of her hand so as not to forget.

oneOf.narrate: Ilse has the printer's proof beside her, to check the type against the page letter by letter. She has found two mistakes already, and gone up to the print shop in her nightgown to say so.
The account goes up to Highpass under seal in the morning, and Ilse means to have every page of it copied before the rider comes for it.
Ailith's cart goes at first light, and Ilse means to have every page copied before then. She has told Ailith so twice.

lines.narrate: For an hour they work in silence. Then Ilse looks up.

lines.text: You join your f's to the next letter.
Everyone does.
Nobody does. Not here. Not for eight hundred years.

lines.narrate: Rue looks at Ilse's page for a while. Then she goes back to her own and joins the next f, and then, after a moment's thought, does not join the one after it.

By the second hour Ilse is joining her f's. By the third Rue has started leaving a space after her full stops the way Ilse does, and Ilse has started squaring off her g's, and neither of them has said a word about it.
Maren comes down at midnight with two cups, and puts one at each end of the table, and sits on the cellar stairs to watch them, and does not interrupt.
At dawn they swap pages to check each other's copies, and for a moment neither of them can tell whose is whose.

lines.text: This one is mine.
That one's mine. Look at the f.
Yes. That is what I mean.

choices.label: Stay and trim the lamps for them

lines.narrate: You trim the lamps for them until the window over the stairs goes grey. Neither of them looks up.

choices.label: Go up and sleep

lines.narrate: You go up and sleep at the inn. When you come down in the morning the two of them are asleep at the long table, one at each end, with their heads on their copies.
That night Linus Pardew comes to Dera's forge with his fiddle, a clean broadsheet and a stub of pencil, and asks whether he may sit. Dera says he may sit if he stops singing. He sits.

oneOf.text: I want the true one. I mean it. I watched a village ring its own pans last night, and there wasn't a sword of light in it anywhere, and it was better. I want to write that. I want the verses right.

I want the true one. I mean it. I stood on that well last night and watched you fight the white at the Briarwood end with a village in its nightclothes behind you, and there wasn't a sword of light in it anywhere. I want to write that. I want the verses right.
And the quiet night. The first town in the free wards. That's a verse on its own, if I can find a rhyme for 'share' that isn't 'there'.
And a boy who wrote his village's rule himself, in letters an inch high. I've that verse already. I wrote it this afternoon and it made me cry, which is a bad sign in a man of my trade.
And the watch kept every night, as it always was. Nobody wants a song about a thing staying the same. I'll make them want one.

lines.text: Now. Orin the Bold. Sir. Would you give me your own verse, in your own words? However you'd like to be sung.

lines.narrate: Orin puts down the cup Dera gave him. Everyone at the forge looks at him. He looks at the fire for a while.

lines.text: The ford at Calder. I was a soldier. I left the farmers on the wrong side of it, and the white had them. Lieutenant Hal went back for them. I didn't.

oneOf.text: Then Briarwatch. Then the council. Then Saltwick. I don't remember it. I gave it away, down there. I know I was tried for it. Write that I was tried.
Then Briarwatch. Then the council. Then Saltwick, where I asked to be tried for what I did there, and was.
Then Briarwatch. Then the council. Then Saltwick, which I'll not tell you about, and you'll not write.

lines.text: I'm six foot. I carry the packs because somebody has to. I've never had a door on my back in my life.

lines.narrate: Linus writes it down, all of it, word for word, with his tongue between his teeth. When Orin stops, he reads it back. It does not rhyme. It is a list of facts, said plainly, by a man who cannot lie.

lines.text: I can't sing that.
No.
I'm going to, though.
And the big one. The one with the door on his back. He's not with you, is he. Is he really eight feet tall?

lines.narrate: You tell Linus that the big one is six feet tall, carries the packs because somebody has to, and has never had a door on his back in his life. Linus writes it down, and crosses out the eight, and sits looking at what is left.

lines.text: That's worse for the song and better for the man.
Put in that he came back. Whoever's in it. That they all came back. That's the verse I'd want, if it was mine.

choices.label: Ask Linus to play the true one, as far as he has it

lines.narrate: He plays it. It is two verses and a half, and the half is the line about the pans, and it does not scan. Dera sings the last line with him under her breath, and then says she did not.

choices.label: Leave them to it, and go up to bed

lines.narrate: You leave them at the forge, Linus with his pencil and Dera with her arms folded, arguing about whether a smith's hammer can rhyme with anything. When you look back from the inn door the forge is still lit.

company-camp.location: The north quay, Merrowgate, the night after

oneOf.narrate: That night the north quay is unloading by lamplight, crate by crate, back off the wagons and onto the stones. Coll Haddow carries his own crate home on his shoulder. Bett comes back down to the quay after him, and sits on the bollard by the empty wagons.

That night the council's clerks are on the north quay with lamps, chalking the council's seal on the wagons' tailboards. Coll Haddow is helping them, for wages. Bett is sitting on the bollard by wagon four, watching him.
That night Coll Haddow is loading wagon four by lamplight, for the end of the week. Bett is sitting on the bollard beside it with the roll in her lap, and her name on it in pencil, crossed out.
That night Bett comes down to the north quay and sits on the bollard by the wagons.

lines.narrate: Nessa is sitting on the quay edge beside her with her boots over the water and Biscuit's head on her knee. Bett has been looking at her for some time.

lines.text: You're going north. Up over the peaks. What's it like?
Never been.
Then what's it like?

lines.narrate: Nessa thinks about it for a while. Then she tells her anyway.

lines.text: Cold. Colder than here. White on the ground all year, and not the bad white, the ordinary kind: snow, so deep you walk on top of it. Writing on every door, so you always know whose house it is. People who give away the day they were born and write it on their arm so they can read it back. And dogs. I've decided there are dogs.
You don't know any of that.
No. I'll write and tell you which bits I got right.

lines.narrate: Biscuit thumps his tail once on the stones.
You sit down on the quay edge beside her. She has been waiting for somebody to.

lines.text: You're going north. Up over the peaks. What's it like?

lines.narrate: You tell her you have never been. She asks again, as if that were no answer, and so you tell her what Rue has told you: the white on the ground all year, the writing on every door, the people who write on their own arms so as to read back who they are.

lines.text: Will you write and tell me if it's true?

oneOf.text: Nobody's going now. Not Da, not anybody. He's glad. I can tell he's glad, and he's pretending he isn't, for me.
Da's going on the council's wagons, when the peaks open. He says the council doesn't take girls either. I asked the clerk. The clerk says it's not up to him, it's up to Da.
The clerk crossed me out. Neatly. I watched him do it. Da didn't say anything.

choices.label: Sit with her until her father calls her in

lines.narrate: You sit on the quay until Coll calls her in. She goes slowly, and looks back once at the north end of the harbour.

choices.label: Go up to the inn

lines.narrate: You leave Nessa on the quay with her. When you look back from the top of the steps they are both looking north.
You leave her on the quay. When you look back from the top of the steps she is looking north.

davin-camp.location: Saltwick, the night after the fire

oneOf.narrate: That night Orin sits with Davin on the parapet, with Davin's pack between them and a length of lamp-rope across both their knees.
That night Orin sits with Davin on the parapet with a length of lamp-rope across both their knees. The pack is unpacked. Davin has not said a word to him since noon, and came up anyway.
That night Davin finds you on the parapet, with his pack and a length of lamp-rope.
That night Davin finds you on the parapet with a length of lamp-rope. The pack is unpacked. He has come up to say something, and has not decided what.
That night Orin sits with Davin on the parapet with a length of lamp-rope across both their knees.

oneOf.text: That's my knot on your pack.
That was my knot on your pack.

lines.text: I learned it off you. From watching.
Then watch again. Slowly.

lines.narrate: He ties it on the parapet rail, slowly, so that Davin can see each turn: a round turn, two half-hitches, and the stopper.

lines.text: It's nearly it. The stopper goes on the other side. Like that it holds the lamp, but it won't come undone when you want it to. Gran ties it the other way, so you can get a lamp off in the dark with one hand. Watch.

lines.narrate: He ties it again, the other way. Orin looks at it for a long time. Then he unties it, and ties it himself, Davin's way, twice, and tugs it.

lines.text: Your way.
Tomorrow, then. The rear of the column. You stay where I can see you.
Where you can see me.
They'll want somebody on the far roofs who ties it right.
They've got somebody.

lines.narrate: He shows you the knot on his pack: a round turn, two half-hitches and a stopper, with the stopper on the far side, so that it comes off in the dark with one hand. His grandmother ties it that way. He shows you twice, until you have it.

lines.text: Everybody ties it wrong. They tie it the soldiers' way, so it holds. It's meant to hold and let go. That's the whole trick of it.
I'll tie yours, on the road. Every morning. You'll see.

lines.narrate: Mags comes up the ladder before it is quite dark, to look at the knot. She looks at it for a while, and nods, and goes down again. She has not said a word about what she said at noon, and nobody has asked her to.

choices.label: Ask Davin to show you too

lines.narrate: He shows you. It takes you four tries, and he does not laugh at any of them.

choices.label: Go round the lamps with him at midnight

lines.narrate: You go round the long planks with him at midnight, lamp by lamp. He checks every knot, and reties two of them.

book-camp.location: The quartermaster's office, Highpass, the night after

oneOf.narrate: That night Quartermaster Iona finds Rue on the step of her office with her book under her arm, and asks her in out of the wind.
That night Quartermaster Iona finds Rue on the step of her office with her book, and the new first page in it, and asks her in out of the wind.
That night Quartermaster Iona finds Rue on the step of her office with nothing in her hands, and asks her in out of the wind.
That night Quartermaster Iona finds Rue on the step of her office, and asks her in out of the wind.

lines.text: I keep ledgers. I've kept Highpass's since before you were born, and the council's since there was a council. I'd like to see yours, if I may.

oneOf.narrate: Rue pushes back her sleeve and shows Iona her wrist, with the one word on it. Iona looks at it as carefully as she looks at anything. Then she takes a new ledger off her shelf, a good one, bound, with nothing in it, and puts it on the table between them, and does not say what it is for. Rue writes the date on the first leaf, and under it, HEATH.
Rue puts her book on the table, and Iona puts the council's ledger beside it, and they read each other's for an hour without speaking.

lines.text: You've no column for what's owed.
Nothing is owed. Things are given. Then they are written down, so that nobody forgets they were given.
Here it's the other way about. Nothing's given. Everything's owed, and written down so that nobody forgets they owe it.
And I've Cass Ord's bill in that case, for forty wagons and a ship, to the copper. That one I'm paying.

oneOf.narrate: Iona takes a sheet off the top of the pile at her elbow: the bill for the watch's night at the north gate, made out to the carter. She reads it over once, and puts it in the stove.
Iona takes a sheet off the top of the pile at her elbow: the bill for the north gate's new timbers, made out to the carter. She reads it over once, and puts it in the stove.

lines.text: Given. Write that down.

lines.narrate: Rue writes it down.
Maren is on the bench by the stove. She has not said anything for an hour.

lines.text: She means it. I can hear that much.
I should hope so. I don't say things twice.

choices.label: Ask Rue what she wrote

lines.text: The quartermaster gave a thing. I wrote it under her name. Tomorrow I will write it on her door. She does not know yet.

choices.label: Leave them to their ledgers

lines.narrate: You leave them at it. The lamp in Iona's window is still lit when the watch changes at midnight.

key-camp.location: The casting hall, Cinder Fold, the night after

lines.narrate: Biscuit would not go near the founders' hatch. When it came up he sat down on the lid with all four legs set and his ears flat, and nothing would shift him, and in the end Nessa picked him up, grey muzzle and all, and carried him across the lid to the casting hall door under one arm, with the lid moving under her boots.
Now he is lying across the hall door with his nose on his paws, watching the lid, and Nessa is sitting beside him.

lines.text: Coward. Great soft coward. Wouldn't go near it. Had to be carried, like a sack of meal, in front of the whole town.

lines.narrate: She says it into his neck, with both arms round him.

lines.text: He was right, mind. He's always right about holes.

oneOf.narrate: Hew comes down from the signal house at half past midnight with the key round his neck, and sits down on Biscuit's other side, and Biscuit puts his head on Hew's knee instead of Nessa's.
Hew comes in off the lid at midnight with his hearth bell, and sits down on Biscuit's other side, and Biscuit puts his head on Hew's knee instead of Nessa's.

lines.text: Traitor.

lines.narrate: She watches the two of them for a while.

lines.text: He's old. The peaks'll be cold, and the Wold's colder, Rue says, and he won't go near a hole, and I bet it's all holes up there. When we go north, he stays here. With Hew. If Hew'll have him.
I'll have him.

oneOf.text: He'll go up the stair with you every night. He'll want to. Let him.
He can sit under the lamp-room for me, since there's nobody up it. Somebody should mind it, even dark.
You'll both go up the stair with whoever's keeping the key, every night. Count the steps for me.

lines.narrate: The family from Wem are asleep in miners' blankets by the forge fire. Hew sits up with them on the hall step with his hearth bell in his lap, and keeps very still so as not to wake the child.

lines.text: I'll go up the stair with them again tomorrow. Somebody has to learn it. I'm learning it.

choices.label: Sit by the hall door

lines.narrate: You sit by the hall door with them until the forge fire is low. Biscuit falls asleep across the feet of all three of you.
You sit by the forge fire until it is low. Hew falls asleep sitting up, with the bell in his lap.

choices.label: Go out and listen to the nine

oneOf.narrate: You go out onto the lid at the turn of the hour and listen to the nine ring it, and the tenth a beat ahead of them. They are in time.
You go out onto the lid at the turn of the hour and listen to the nine ring it. They are in time.

letters-camp.location: The vault under the drill-yard, Vell, the night after

stair.title: At the Top of the Stair

oneOf.narrate: That night the satchel sits on the vault table under Fennick's lamp, tied with red tape, and nobody touches it.
That night the vault is quiet. Fennick and his clerks are still at the bottom of the stair, copying, and will be for a week.
That night you sit at the vault table and try to remember what you wrote, and cannot.

lines.narrate: You are not as tired as you should be. Nobody says so at first.

lines.text: A day of stair, up, in armour, and you came out at the top like you'd walked across a yard. I've done stairs in armour. I sat down at the top of every one. The old guard-books call that Iron Hide, when the body stops minding.

lines.narrate: A day of stair, up, in armour, and you come out at the top as if you had walked across a yard. The old guard-books call that Iron Hide: the body has stopped minding.

lines.text: You trimmed the lamp wick with your knife on the stair. One cut, in the dark, and you never looked. That's a Blademaster's hand. Keen Edge. The edge goes where you want it before you've thought it.

lines.narrate: On the stair you trim the lamp wick with your knife, one cut, in the dark, without looking. A Blademaster's hand: Keen Edge, the edge going where you want it before you have thought it.

lines.text: On the floor, Fennick's clerks did what you said without looking round to see who'd said it. That's the thing. Not the voice. When people stop checking. Veteran Captain, the old companies called it. Banner Captains have it.

lines.narrate: On the floor, Fennick's clerks did what you told them without looking round to see who had said it. The old companies called that Veteran Captain: people stop checking.

lines.text: I lost you on the stair today. Twice. I was right behind you with a lamp. Blade in the Dark, the Nightblades call that. I'm the one who goes first. I don't like not knowing where you are.

lines.narrate: On the stair the lamp behind you loses you twice, and finds you again ahead of it. Blade in the Dark, the Nightblades call that.

lines.text: You mended Fennick's lamp on the way up with a hairpin and a bit of his red tape, and it burns better than it did new. Master Tinker. That's Trapwright work. I'm keeping the hairpin.

lines.narrate: On the way up you mend Fennick's lamp with a hairpin and a length of his red tape, and it burns better than it did new. Master Tinker: Trapwright work.

lines.text: Two of Fennick's clerks told you, separately, what the other one was afraid of, and neither of them meant to. You have people now. Everywhere you go. Informants, the Spymasters say. I'd like to know which of them is me.

lines.narrate: Two of Fennick's clerks tell you, separately, what the other one is afraid of, and neither of them means to. A Spymaster has people everywhere: Informants.

lines.text: Your lamp went out on the stair and you lit it again off your own fingers. You didn't even think about it. The hair on my arms stood up. Overchannel, the Stormcallers call it. Warn me next time.

lines.narrate: Your lamp goes out on the stair and you light it again off your own fingers without thinking. Overchannel, the Stormcallers call it.

lines.text: You caught Fennick's box before it fell. Before. I saw your hand move, and then I saw the box start to go. Temporal Poise, the Timeweavers call that. I'm not going to think about it too hard.

lines.narrate: You catch Fennick's box on the stair before it starts to fall. Temporal Poise, the Timeweavers call that: the hand moves first.

lines.text: Whatever you call up, it's stronger now. I felt it on the stair, behind you, like a wall at my back. Pact Strength, isn't it? The Summoners' word. I'd like it to stay on our side.

lines.narrate: Whatever you call up is stronger now. On the stair you can feel it behind you like a wall. Pact Strength, the Summoners call it.

lines.text: You put your hand on that clerk's head, the one who forgot his sister's name, and he stopped shaking. Blessed Hands. The Menders of Hosts have it. I've sat with a lot of people who were shaking. I've never once done that.

lines.narrate: You put your hand on the head of the clerk who forgot his sister's name, and he stops shaking. Blessed Hands, the Menders of Hosts call it.

lines.text: When the white came up off the floor you looked at it the way I look at somebody who's lying to me. Inquisitor's Zeal. I don't know if I find that comforting.

lines.narrate: When the white came up off the floor you looked at it the way you look at a liar. Inquisitor's Zeal, the old orders call it.

lines.text: There's a warmth off your mail. I noticed it on the stair, standing next to you in the cold. Consecrated Plate, the Templars call it. I'd stand next to you on a cold night again.

lines.narrate: There is a warmth off your mail that the stair could not take out of it. Consecrated Plate, the Templars call it.

lines.text: Every rat on that stair got out of your way. Not running. Getting out of your way, like you were the big one. Alpha Bond, isn't it? I've never seen a rat step aside before.

lines.narrate: Every rat on the stair gets out of your way: not running, stepping aside, as if you were the big one. Alpha Bond, the Beastbond call it.

lines.text: You saw the bottom of the stair from a hundred steps up. I watched you do it. I've got the best eyes in Cinder Fold, and I couldn't. Longshot. Fine. You can go first. For looking.

lines.narrate: From a hundred steps up you can see the bottom of the stair, when nobody else can see past the lamp. Longshot.

lines.text: A day of stair down and a day up, and you're not even tired. Seasoned Traveller, the Wayfinders call that. You'll want it, north.

lines.narrate: A day of stair down and a day up, and you are not even tired. Seasoned Traveller, the Wayfinders call it.

lines.text: On the floor today you talked to Fennick about the founders' spelling, and he took notes. From you. Vast Learning, the Loremasters call it. I've never seen that clerk take notes from anybody.

lines.narrate: On the floor, Fennick asks you about the founders' spelling, and takes notes. Vast Learning, the Loremasters call it.

lines.text: You were humming on the stair. A whole day of it, up. And every one of us kept your time and never felt the steps. Rousing Voice. The Warchanters have it. Hum it again tomorrow.

lines.narrate: You hum on the stair, a whole day of it, up, and nobody behind you feels the steps. Rousing Voice, the Warchanters call it.

lines.text: Fennick, the clerks, whoever's on the door. They all tell you things they wouldn't tell each other, and nobody minds. Diplomatic Immunity, they call that in Merrowgate, and they mean it as a joke. It isn't one.

lines.narrate: Fennick, the clerks, whoever is on the door: they all tell you things they would not tell each other, and nobody minds. Diplomatic Immunity, the Diplomats call it.
Somewhere on the stair today you stopped counting the steps. You are not sure when.

choices.label: Go up and listen to the bells

oneOf.narrate: You go up onto the wall and listen to the fifty gate-bells ring the hour over an empty city.
You go up onto the wall. The gate-bells ring the hour. The great bell in the heart of the city does not.
You go up onto the wall and listen to Vell's bells ring the hour.

choices.label: Sleep by the vault stove

lines.narrate: You sleep by the stove in the vault, with the iron door below you, and dream of a floor that goes on further than any lamp.

embassy-camp.location: Brannagh's lodging, Highpass, the night after the vote

lines.narrate: Brannagh has the Fenmere delegates round her kitchen table the night after the vote, and you with them, and a pot of barley on the fire.

oneOf.text: Well. You're ours now. Seal and all. Don't lose it; Iona will charge you.
Well. You're your own. I'd not have voted for it. I'd not have voted against it either.
Well. Ten thousand beds. Fenmere's got about forty. I'll find more.

lines.narrate: She ladles barley into bowls for a while without saying anything.

lines.text: Are there goats? Up there. In the north.

lines.narrate: Nobody knows.

lines.text: I do not know. I have not written it down. If there are, they will have their names on them.
There's always goats. Everywhere's got goats.
Then I'll get on with them.
I only ask. You can tell a lot about people from whether they keep goats. Fenmere's kept goats since before the bells. If they keep them up there, I'll know what to say first.

lines.narrate: Out of the window, the peaks above the pass are white to the saddle. The Hall of Legends is up there in the dark, under the first of the snow.

choices.label: Eat the barley

lines.narrate: You eat the barley. Brannagh fills your bowl again before it is empty, and the Fenmere delegates argue about the vote until the fire is low.

choices.label: Watch the peaks from the window

lines.narrate: You watch the peaks until the cloud comes down over the saddle. In a few days you will be up there.

b4-partone-end.location: The north door of the Hall of Legends

lines.narrate: Evening at the north door. You make camp in the lee of the Wold's nine, out of the wind, with the Wold under its cloud below you and the free wards behind you under the snow, and nobody wants to sleep.
Rue asks, the way the Wold asks at a door, what you are bringing. Not what is in your pack. What you are bringing.

oneOf.text: Davin. And the knot on his pack, which is Mags's. And a soldier who'd like to be asked in, this time.
A soldier who'd like to be asked in, this time. That's all. It's enough to be going on with.
Ears. And a door I can't see the colour of any more, so I'll know what it costs when they give. I'll hear whether they mean it, and whether we do.
Ears. I'll hear whether they mean it, and whether we do.
The key. A light, if they want one.
Me. First through every door. That's what I'm for.

lines.narrate: Rue writes in her book, on a new page, a line at a time.

lines.text: Lamps. I brought six. Nobody asked me to.
And you?

choices.label: Tell her what you are bringing

oneOf.narrate: You tell her: the free wards' word, under its seal, and whatever it will cost Iona.
You tell her: a door open in the south for anyone who wants it, and ten thousand beds that nobody has found yet.
You tell her: yourself, and your own word, and nothing in writing.

lines.text: I have written it down.

lines.narrate: Before dark Linus comes through the Hall from the south door with his guide, to go back down while there is light. Before he goes he stands at the north door with his writing case open and reads you the first verse, so that somebody who was there has heard it.

oneOf.narrate: 'Nine on the south face with bells in their hands, and nine on the north with none, and a bell in the middle, small as a bucket, that rang once, and every bell in the south answered it. And these went down to knock.'

'Nine on the south face with bells in their hands, and nine on the north with none, and a bell in the middle, small as a bucket. And one of these knelt at the north door and gave, and went down to knock.'
'Nine on the south face with bells in their hands, and nine on the north with none, and a bell in the middle, small as a bucket, that nobody rang. And these went quietly down to knock.'

lines.text: That's true. All of it. Dera can't cross out a word. First time in twenty years.
I'll sing it in Briarwatch at midwinter. Come back and tell me the next one.

lines.narrate: He goes back through the Hall and down the south side into the snow, with the guide carrying his case, and turns round twice to wave.
Below the north door the road goes down into the cloud.

choices.label: Look down at the road into the Wold

lines.narrate: You look down at the road for a long time. Tomorrow, the Wold.

lantry-camp.location: Teasel's kitchen, Lantry, the night after the giving

oneOf.narrate: Teasel's kitchen, the night after the giving. The town is quiet. Teasel is at the table chalking tomorrow's doors on a slate, and Rue is by the wall with her book under her arm, nearly asleep.

Teasel's kitchen, the night after the pots. The town is very quiet, the way a house is quiet after an argument. Teasel is at the table, writing on a slate what she will read in the morning, and rubbing it out, and writing it again.
Teasel's kitchen, the night after the giving. Nobody says much. Teasel is at the table writing tomorrow's doors on a slate, and the smith's is the first.

lines.narrate: Nessa borrows a sheet of Teasel's paper and a stub of lead and sits on the floor by the stove with her back to the room, and writes a letter. It takes her a long time. She does not let anyone see it.

When it is done she folds it small and writes on the outside, in capitals: 'BISCUIT. HIGHPASS. THE GUARDROOM, BY THE BRAZIER.' Then she reads it, the inside, to herself, moving her lips, and nobody else.

lines.text: Who is Biscuit?
My dog. He's old. He couldn't do the saddle. He'll not get it. Nobody's carrying letters over the peaks in this. I know that.
Then why write it?
So it's written. You'd know about that.

lines.narrate: Rue looks at her for a while. Then she opens her book at a new page, and writes something, and turns it round so that Nessa can read it. Nessa reads it, and goes red, and puts the letter inside her shirt next to the key.

Rue looks at her for a while. Then she opens her book at a new page, and writes something, and turns it round so that Nessa can read it. Nessa reads it, and goes red, and puts the letter inside her shirt.

oneOf.narrate: Rue sits by the stove with her book open, reading back over the day, and writes a line at the bottom of the page, and turns it round so that you can read it: 'The southerners came down the old road, and stayed the night.'
Rue sits by the stove with her book open, reading back over the day, and writes a line at the bottom of the page, and turns it round so that you can read it: 'The southerners stayed for the giving.'

choices.label: Sleep by the stove

lines.narrate: You sleep by Teasel's stove. In the morning she reads you your own door: the top door's, with your names on it now, in the children's hand, and one of them spelt wrong.

choices.label: Read the doors in the street before you sleep

lines.narrate: You go out and read the doors down the street by lamplight, every one, and come back in, and find that you have already forgotten the first ones.

sheddon-camp.location: The porch of the Long Hall, Orme, the night Sheddon came in

lines.narrate: Orme has taken Sheddon in for the night in the porch of the Long Hall, two hundred people on straw under the lamps, and the Hall's clerks going along the rows writing everyone's name on a board by their head.

oneOf.narrate: Sedge's mother is asleep on the straw with her coat still on. Sedge sits beside her, with his back to the wall, and does not sleep.
Sedge sits against the wall by himself, with his sleeve pushed up, reading his own arm.

lines.narrate: Orin sits on the porch step outside, in the cold, with his elbows on his knees. After a while you go and sit with him.

oneOf.text: Varn said the contract was the salt. Today I said the contract was two hundred. Same words. Same order. I understand him now. I didn't, all these years. I do now.

Varn wouldn't have gone back. A captain who goes back has left his column. I know that. I did it anyway, and gave you mine, and lost the name of his. I understand him better than I did this morning. That's the worst of it.

I was going to say 'on'. I had it in my mouth. You went before I could. I'm glad. I'm angry, and I'm glad. I understand Varn now. Someone has to stand at the front and not go back. I didn't know how much it weighed.

lines.text: I don't forgive him. Understanding's not the same. He went over the ridge and never once asked whose town it was. I knew whose mother she was. That's the difference. It's not much. It's what I've got.

oneOf.text: You came back. With her. Gran would've said that's the whole job.
You did all right. At the front. Gran would've said.

lines.text: Go to sleep, Davin.

lines.narrate: Rue sits a little way along the porch with her book, and writes the day into it, and does not read any of it back to anyone.

When she has done, she turns the book round so that you can read the last line: 'At the farm-track cairn the southerner said on. Sedge went on.' She does not say anything about it. She has written it.

choices.label: Sit on the step until the lamps go down

lines.narrate: You sit on the step until the Hall's lamps are turned down, one by one, and the porch is asleep.

choices.label: Find a place on the straw

lines.narrate: You find a place on the straw between two Sheddon families, and a clerk writes your name on the board by your head, and asks you to spell it.

orme-camp.location: Burdock's desk in the Long Hall, Orme, after midnight

lines.narrate: After midnight the Long Hall is nearly empty. Burdock is still at his desk, because the day is not finished until everyone in it is written, and he has not finished you.

oneOf.narrate: The page about the south lies open beside him, the whole of it, bells and all, and every so often he stops and reads a line of it again, and believes it a little more.
The page about the south lies open beside him in its two columns, and every so often he reads a line across from one column to the other, and nods.
The page about the south lies open beside him with two lines on it: 'The south: not yet.' And under it, in the Reckoner's hand, the nine hundred years. He has not turned the page.

lines.text: Each of you. Properly. Not just 'southerners'. Name, and town, and one thing about you that is true, so that whoever reads it after me knows you.
Orin Stoneward. Of Briarwatch, I suppose. Write that I carried a lantern once and I'm sorry for it.
'Sorry for it.' Good. People are always glad to read that somebody was sorry.
Maren Vale. Of the Sisters' house. Write that I listen. Don't write what I hear.
Nessa Reed. Cinder Fold. Write that I go first. And Biscuit.
Biscuit. Is that a person?
He's my dog. He's at Highpass.
How do you spell Biscuit?

lines.narrate: Nessa spells it for him, one letter at a time, and he writes it as she says it, and blots it.

lines.text: Grey at the mouth. Kind. Put that, Burdock. Nessa told me in Lantry, and I wrote it down.

lines.narrate: Burdock writes it. He reads the line back aloud: 'Biscuit, a dog, of Highpass, grey at the mouth, kind.' Then he looks up, and believes in Biscuit completely, and asks whether he will be coming north.

lines.text: Davin. Saltwick. I do the lamps. Write that I held the rear.
Davin. Saltwick. I do the lamps.

lines.narrate: Then it is you. Burdock waits with his pen. You tell him your name, and your town, and he asks for the one true thing, and you have to think about it for a long time.

lines.text: You are the letter. I have it on the wall. 'We are coming north, to ask properly.' I shall write: came, as it said.

choices.label: Tell him the one true thing

lines.narrate: You tell him. He writes it, and reads it back to you, and it sounds truer in his voice than it did in yours.

choices.label: Ask him to choose it for you

lines.narrate: You ask him to choose. He looks at you for a while over both pairs of spectacles, and writes: 'Came from the south, and asked.' Then he reads it back, and is satisfied.

greve-camp.location: Yarrow's kitchen, Greve, the night after the giving

oneOf.narrate: Yarrow's kitchen, late. The censer is on the shelf over the fire, not lit, and Yarrow keeps looking at it.
Yarrow's kitchen, late. The house-book is on the table, open at a clean page, and the slates have gone down the valley to Orme.
Yarrow's kitchen, late. The censer is on its chain by the door, cleaned and ready for the next giving.

lines.text: Your soup needs salt.
My soup is the best soup in the valley. Yours, I'm told, is a danger to the young.
Rue told you that.
Rue wrote it down, which is worse.

lines.narrate: They go on like that all evening, over the soup, and then over the house-book, and then over a woman from up the valley whose hands shake, and what to give her for it. Maren says willow bark. Yarrow says nettle and patience. They agree about nothing and they do not stop talking.

oneOf.text: You'll have cost me half my house. They'll not come to be given to if they can't give. They'll come to sit, I suppose. I can do sitting.
Burdock's sent back for more names. I've written him every one I can remember from thirty years, and I can't remember many. That's my fault and the house's.
I'll light it at the next giving, and they'll give, and go home. I'll not pretend I'm not glad.
You're very good at this. I want that written down somewhere, by somebody who'll remember it.

oneOf.narrate: Yarrow sits with you by the fire until the lamp burns down, and tells you about the people who have sat on her benches, as many as she can remember. It is not many.

lines.text: I'll remember you were good company. For a season. It's a long time, a season, when you're grieving.

choices.label: Sit up with them until the lamp burns down

lines.narrate: You sit up by the fire until the lamp burns down, and the house is quiet, and nobody on the benches gets up in the night.

choices.label: Sleep on the end bench by the door

lines.narrate: You sleep on the end bench by the door, where you read the names from, and wake once in the night to hear somebody on the next bench saying one over to themselves, quietly, so as to have it in the morning.

thrum-nessa.location: Heath's door step, Thrum, the night after

lines.narrate: Night on Heath's step. The lamp over the door is lit. Inside, Heath and Furze are asleep, and the bread is set to rise for the morning.

oneOf.narrate: Rue and Nessa are sitting on the step under the lamp with a blanket round both of them, and Rue's book open across both their knees.
Rue is sitting on the step under the lamp with a blanket round her shoulders and her book open on her knees, and she moves over to make room for you.

oneOf.text: Read me who she is. I have it in here. I would like to hear it from somebody who does not know her either.
It hurts. You did not say it would hurt this much. I am glad you did not say. I would have given it.

lines.text: Give it here, then.

lines.narrate: Nessa reads Rue's mother to her by the lamp, slowly, the page with Heath's bread and Heath's hands on it, stumbling on the long words, and Rue listens with her head on one side, interested and not hurt at all.
There is one word to read. Nessa reads it off Rue's wrist, 'Heath', and then makes up the rest, a page of it, out loud, about the bread, and Rue lets her.
You read Rue her mother, slowly, by the lamp, and she listens with her head on one side, interested and not hurt at all.

There is one word to read. You read it off Rue's wrist, 'Heath', and then you tell her what you saw Heath do today, at the table, with the bread and with Furze's chalk, and she listens with her head on one side, interested and not hurt at all.

lines.text: Course it hurts. That's how you know it's still in there.

lines.narrate: Rue writes in her book by the lamp for a long time. When she has finished she turns it round so that you can read it: 'Kept. It hurts. Somebody went back for me.'

lines.text: You answered me. Nobody in the Wold would have. They would have said, it is yours, and gone in. You said it anyway. I have written down what you said, in your words, so that I can read it every morning.
Don't read it every morning. Read it on the bad ones.
I'm writing to Biscuit tonight. I'm going to tell him about your brother. He'd like your brother. He likes anybody with chalk on them.
Tell him I said hello. Write it in capitals. He will not be able to read it, but it is polite.
Davin trimmed her lamp. Nobody asked him. Write that down for me tomorrow, in case I forget to.

choices.label: Sit on the step until the lamp needs trimming

lines.narrate: You sit on the step until the lamp needs trimming, and trim it, and the lane is quiet all night to the third door.

choices.label: Go in, and leave them the step

lines.narrate: You go in, and leave the step to them. Through the door you can hear them talking until very late, and then not talking, and the lamp still lit.

reckoning-camp.location: The Long Hall's yard, Orme, before dawn

lines.narrate: Before dawn the Long Hall's yard is empty and blue, with the snow trodden flat round the pump, and the post the tally-guard drill at standing in the middle.

oneOf.narrate: Through the window Sloe is at her table, copying her sum onto a second slate, for the council, in case the first is lost on the road.
Through the window Sloe is at her table, reading the promise at the foot of her slate, over and over, as if it were a sum she could not get to come out.
Through the window Sloe is at her table, writing her own name and town on the inside of her left arm, the way Rue does, for the road.

lines.text: You were in the yard before it was light, with your shield up, putting your whole weight behind the rim into a post. The post moved. Shield Slam, the old guard-books call that. I'd not want to be the post.

lines.narrate: In the yard before it is light, you put your whole weight behind the rim of your shield into a post, and the post moves. Shield Slam, the old guard-books call it.

lines.text: Three cuts at the yard post before I'd blinked. Three. I counted the marks after. Thousand Cuts, the Blademasters call it. I'm not standing near that post again.

lines.narrate: In the yard before it is light, you put three cuts into the post before the first has finished ringing. Thousand Cuts, the Blademasters call it.

lines.text: You had the clerks in the yard this morning, two from the left and two from the right, round the post, on a word. They didn't even know they'd done it. Pincer Command. The Banner Captains had it. I never saw it done this well.

lines.narrate: In the yard before it is light, you put two clerks on the left of the post and two on the right with one word, and they go without knowing they have. Pincer Command, the Banner Captains call it.

lines.text: You hit the yard post twice this morning from the dark side of it, and I was watching, and I didn't see you go round. Shadow Flurry. Nightblade work. Don't do that to me.

lines.narrate: In the yard before it is light, you strike the post twice from the side of it nobody is watching. Shadow Flurry, the Nightblades call it.

lines.text: You blew the frost off the yard wall this morning with a pinch of something and a bit of string, and it went exactly where you said, and nowhere else. Controlled Blast. Trapwright work. Burdock wrote it down as weather.

lines.narrate: In the yard before it is light, a pinch of powder and a length of string blow the frost off the wall exactly where you meant, and nowhere else. Controlled Blast, the Trapwrights call it.

lines.text: Two of the door-bearers told me this morning, separately, that you'd agreed with each of them. You had. Both. Double Cross, the Spymasters say. I'd like you to tell me which of them was true.

lines.narrate: Before it is light, two door-bearers each go away from you sure you agreed with them, and you did, with both. Double Cross, the Spymasters call it.

lines.text: You clapped your hands in the yard this morning and every pane in the Hall rang. Every one. Burdock came out in his nightshirt. Thunderclap, the Stormcallers call it. Warn me next time.

lines.narrate: In the yard before it is light, you clap your hands once and every pane in the Long Hall rings. Thunderclap, the Stormcallers call it.

lines.text: You stopped the snow this morning. In the yard. It hung there, every flake, while you walked through it. Time Stop, the Timeweavers call it. I'm not going to think about it at all.

lines.narrate: In the yard before it is light, the falling snow stops in the air round you, every flake, while you walk through it. Time Stop, the Timeweavers call it.

lines.text: There were more of them this morning. Whatever you call up. A yard full, through a door that wasn't there. Legion of the Gate, the Summoners' word. I'd like them all on our side.

lines.narrate: In the yard before it is light, a door that is not there opens, and the yard fills. Legion of the Gate, the Summoners call it.

lines.text: You stood in the yard this morning with your hands out, and every one of us felt it, at the breakfast table, through the wall. Sanctuary of Hosts. The Menders of Hosts have it. I've never felt anything like it.

lines.narrate: In the yard before it is light, you hold your hands out, and everyone in the Long Hall feels it through the wall. Sanctuary of Hosts, the Menders of Hosts call it.

lines.text: You looked at the yard post this morning and said one word to it, and it went black from the top down. Sentence, the old orders called that. It's a good thing the post wasn't lying.

lines.narrate: In the yard before it is light, you say one word to the post, and it goes black from the top down. Sentence, the old orders call it.

lines.text: You stood in the yard this morning, and every one of us coming out of the Hall stood up straighter. Me too. Aura of Valor, the Templars call it. I'd follow that through a door.

lines.narrate: In the yard before it is light, you stand still, and everyone coming out of the Long Hall stands up straighter. Aura of Valor, the Templars call it.

lines.text: Every dog in Orme was in the yard this morning, sitting round you, waiting for you to say. Call of the Wild, isn't it? Biscuit would have hated it. He'd have come anyway.

lines.narrate: In the yard before it is light, every dog in Orme comes and sits round you, waiting for you to say. Call of the Wild, the Beastbond call it.

lines.text: Two arrows into the yard post this morning, and both of them pinned the same sack to it, and the second went through the first one's fletching. Pinning Shots. Fine. You can go first. For shooting.

lines.narrate: In the yard before it is light, two arrows pin the same sack to the post, the second through the fletching of the first. Pinning Shots, the Deadeyes call it.

lines.text: The tally-guard went round the yard three times this morning looking for you, and you were standing by the pump. They walked past you. Lead Astray, the Wayfinders call it. Do it to the right people.

lines.narrate: In the yard before it is light, the tally-guard go round three times looking for you while you stand by the pump. Lead Astray, the Wayfinders call it.

lines.text: You read the oldest wall aloud in the yard this morning, through the window, and every clerk in the Hall stopped writing to listen. Recital of Ages, the Loremasters call it. Burdock cried.

lines.narrate: Before it is light, you read the oldest wall aloud through the window, and every clerk in the Long Hall stops writing to listen. Recital of Ages, the Loremasters call it.

lines.text: You sang in the yard this morning. Low. And the icicles on the Hall came down all at once, the whole row. Dirge, the Warchanters call it. Sing it somewhere else next time.

lines.narrate: In the yard before it is light, you sing one low line, and every icicle on the Long Hall comes down at once. Dirge, the Warchanters call it.

lines.text: Half the door-bearers came to breakfast this morning with a promise to keep for you, and not one of them could say when you'd asked. Alliance, they call that in Merrowgate. They're not wrong.

lines.narrate: Before it is light, half the door-bearers come to breakfast each with a promise to keep for you, and none of them can say when you asked. Alliance, the Diplomats call it.
In the yard before it is light, you go through your drill at the post, the same as every morning, and nothing about it is new. You are not sure when it stopped being hard.

lines.text: I wrote down what I saw you do. I do not know what it is called. I have left a space for the name.

choices.label: Do it again, now that it has been seen

lines.narrate: You do it again in the blue light, slowly, so that whoever is watching can see how. Then you go in to the fire.

choices.label: Go in to the fire

lines.narrate: You go in to the fire in the Long Hall, where Burdock is already at his desk, writing the morning.

potbells-camp.location: Under Dunnet's bell-frame, the night after

oneOf.narrate: Dunnet's street, late. The bell-frame is empty, and the pieces of the bell are stacked by the smithy door to be made into pots again. Campion is sitting in the empty frame with her mother's pan-handle across her knees.
Dunnet's street, late. The bell hangs in its frame. Down the shelf, Wem's street is dark, with nobody in it. Campion is sitting on the step under the frame with the rope across her knees.

The boundary stones, late. The bell-frame stands over the middle stone with the rota chalked on it, and a lamp from each village hung on the frame. Campion is sitting on the stone, on the Dunnet side, next to a boy from Wem who is asleep.

lines.text: You know how to ring properly. In the south. Everybody says so. Teach me.

oneOf.text: I know there's no bell. I know why. I'd still like to know how. In case. In case one day there's one that doesn't send it anywhere.
I'm ringing it every night now, whatever happens. I'd like to ring it so it's not ugly. If it's going to be rung.
Half the nights it's going to be rung onto us. On those nights I want it rung properly. I'm not having Wem's boy say I can't count.

lines.text: I will write down whatever you teach her, so that she has it after the season.

oneOf.text: Don't look at me. I go up towers and light lamps. Wren's in a bell. That's as near as I get.
Don't look at me. I go up towers and light lamps. Wren did the bells.

lines.text: I can tie the rope so it doesn't slip. That's all I've got.

lines.narrate: Campion waits, with her burnt hands round her knees, looking at you.

choices.label: Teach her to ring: the pull, the catch, and where the note goes

lines.narrate: You show her the pull, and the catch on the sally, and how to let the rope go up without fighting it. Then you show her where the note goes, with your arm, down the valley, and she watches your arm for a long time, and nods, and writes it on her own.

choices.label: Tell her first where away is

lines.narrate: You tell her where away is. Not Wem: further. Over the peaks, nine hundred years, every bell in the south. She listens to all of it with her hands round her knees, and at the end she says, 'Then teach me anyway. Somebody should know how, who knows where.'

hush-camp.location: The last cairn north of Orme, the first night south

oneOf.narrate: The first night south, at the last cairn, late. The walkers are asleep round it in a ring, close together, holding hands. Nobody else is asleep.
The first night south, at the last cairn, late. Behind you to the north the marks go back into the white, one every twenty paces. Nobody is asleep.
The first night south, at the last cairn, late. The cairn road runs south from it under a white that was not there yesterday. Nobody is asleep.

lines.narrate: Nobody says anything for a long time. Then Rue takes out her chalk and writes a name on the cairn, small, and says it aloud, so that it has been said.

oneOf.text: Heath. I do not remember her. I have it written. I am keeping the name.
Heath. I am keeping her.
Sedge's mother. She hasn't got one. I'm keeping that she hadn't.
Davin.
Mags.

lines.text: Anwen.
Wren.

lines.narrate: Rue writes each one on the cairn as it is said, under her own, and then holds out the chalk to you.

choices.label: Say your own name

lines.narrate: You say your own name, aloud, into the quiet, and Rue writes it on the cairn with the others.

choices.label: Say the name of someone you have lost

lines.narrate: You say a name, aloud, into the quiet. Rue writes it on the cairn with the others, and does not ask whose it was.

column-camp._note: column-camp must keep an empty cast: a scene whose cast is not all in the party is skipped by skipTo, which goes to town and would bypass world.goingOn, so chapter 20 would not open straight after it.
column-camp.location: Under the overhang on the north face, the night after

oneOf.narrate: Late, under the overhang. The column sleeps roped, in rows along the road, and the sledges are lashed to iron rings in the rock that somebody cut nine hundred years ago. Burdock is awake, sitting on the first of them with a lamp.
Late, under the overhang. The column sleeps roped, in rows along the road. Below, a long way down, a lamp is going down the switchbacks into the white with the sledges. Rue is awake, watching it.

knot-camp.location: The guardroom of the lower watch, Highpass, late

lines.narrate: Late, in the guardroom of the lower watch, by the brazier. The watch are asleep along the walls, and some of the Wold's people with them, in their coats.
Biscuit is asleep against Nessa's boots, grey at the muzzle, with one ear up.
Orin sits by the brazier with a length of rope off the guardroom's coil, and the cut rope from the hook on his knee beside it, and ties the knot from memory.
He ties it slowly. A round turn. Two half-hitches. The stopper. It comes out plain, the way he ties it now, and he looks at it, and unties it.
He ties it again, and works it wrong: the stopper on the wrong side of the hitches, and loose. He unties that too.

The third time his hands go small and hard over the tail without him, and pull the stopper down tight, and it is the knot on the hook. The same. He holds the two side by side in the light of the brazier.

lines.text: There. That's it. I still can't tell you what it's called.
Somebody showed me that once and told me its name, and I said it back to them. I can feel where the name was. Like a tooth that's gone.

lines.narrate: He ties it twice, copying the knot on the hook turn for turn, and pulls the stopper down tight the way the rope families do, and the second time it comes out right.

lines.text: There. I've tied that knot all my life, and never once like that. That's not a soldier's knot. It's a ringer's. I don't know its name either. I never needed it to have one.
You'll get the name back. You got the knot.

lines.narrate: You sit by the brazier with a length of rope off the guardroom's coil and try to tie the knot from the hook, turn for turn. It comes out wrong twice. The third time it is close. It is not the same.
Rue watches from the bench with her book open on her knee.

lines.text: I will draw it. If nobody knows its name, I will write down what it looks like. That is a kind of name.

choices.label: Sleep by the brazier

lines.narrate: You sleep by the brazier. In the morning the knot is still tied on the end of the guardroom's coil, and nobody has untied it.

Where his number and hers disagree, they stop, and find out why.

quietnight-camp.location: The bell-room of Briarwatch's tower, the next night

lines.narrate: The next night, late, you climb the tower with Tovin and Pim for the hour, because you have never once been up there for it in summer.
Tovin takes one rope and Pim the other. They ring the hour together, Pim a breath behind, the way he always has.

oneOf.narrate: The bell is bronze only, and the two notes go out over the fields.
Inside the bell Aster Vey rings with them, a little late, as she always has.

lines.narrate: At the next hour they take the ropes and do not ring. They sit on the bench under the window with the ropes in their laps, and listen.

Out over the fields, at first, there is nothing to hear. Then, very faint, from the south and the east, a bell. Then another, further off. Every town keeps its own hours. You have never heard them all at once before.
Down in the far fields a lamp is lit in one of the Wold's tents, and somebody there begins to read names aloud, slowly, the way the Wold does at a door.

lines.text: That's all of them. Ringing it north. I never heard them before. You don't, when you're ringing.

choices.label: Listen until the next hour

lines.narrate: You listen until the next hour. Then Pim takes up his rope again and looks at Tovin, and Tovin nods, and they ring.

gatehouse-camp.location: The gatehouse wall, Highpass, the night after

lines.narrate: The night after, nobody wants to go to bed, and you sit up on the gatehouse wall under a sky that has not been properly dark all summer, the way you sat up there on the night of the first snow, two winters ago.

oneOf.narrate: Down in the yard the frame stands empty, with nothing on the beam.
Down under the gatehouse the end cell is dark, and its door stands open.
Down in the yard the bell stands in its frame, and now and then, very low, it hums two notes, one after the other, the way a man goes over a lesson.

Down in the yard the bell stands in its frame with the dew on it, and says nothing all night.

lines.text: You carried the watch's full water-butt up the wall stair this morning on one shoulder, and the cut you bound on the cook's hand had closed by supper. Living Fortress, the Bulwark Knights call that. I'd only ever read about it.
